analysis.one_liner: Restarts federal oil and gas leasing, limits presidential leasing bans, and speeds permits for energy projects.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 4 cosponsors on September 29, 2022, the bill was referred to five House committees that never acted on it, and it died without a single hearing or vote when the Congress ended January 3, 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would force the Interior Department to immediately resume and hold frequent oil and gas lease sales on federal land and offshore, including at least four sales a year each in states like Wyoming and New Mexico and two a year each in the Gulf of Mexico and Alaska. It would bar the President from halting or limiting new oil, gas, or coal leasing on federal land without an act of Congress. It would also speed up energy permitting by setting tight deadlines for environmental reviews, letting some drilling and pipeline projects skip parts of that review, and cutting the window for citizens to sue over federal energy permits to 150 days.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies that drill on federal land and offshore would gain the most: guaranteed quarterly lease sales in nine or more states, minimum annual offshore sales in the Gulf and Alaska, mandatory issuance of all pending drilling permits within 30 days, and drilling allowed to proceed while lawsuits are pending. Coal companies would gain protection from any presidential moratorium on new coal leases. Pipeline builders and companies shipping liquefied natural gas by rail would gain faster approvals, weaker state water-quality vetoes, and a much shorter window for opponents to sue. Renewable, geothermal, and transmission developers would also gain faster rights-of-way and exemptions from environmental review for maintenance and upgrades.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Oil, gas, coal, and pipeline companies

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Interior Department to immediately resume onshore lease sales and hold at least four oil and gas lease sales a year in each qualifying state (Wyoming, New Mexico, Colorado, Utah, Montana, North Dakota, Oklahoma, Nevada and others), offering all eligible parcels.
Requires at least two Gulf of Mexico lease sales and two Alaska offshore lease sales a year, and completes all remaining sales from the 2017-2022 offshore program by September 30, 2023.
Bars the President from blocking or delaying new oil, gas, and coal leases, permits, or withdrawals of federal land from energy development unless Congress passes a law authorizing it.
Orders Interior to issue all pending applications for permits to drill that meet statutory deadlines within 30 days of enactment, and lets permitting continue despite unrelated pending lawsuits.

Streamlines permitting for all energy types: one-year deadlines for environmental assessments and two-year deadlines for environmental impact statements, reuse of prior reviews for similar projects, categorical exclusions for transmission maintenance and renewable projects, 50-year right-of-way terms, and a 60-day deadline to flag incomplete right-of-way applications.

Allows oil and gas drilling on private surface land with less than 50% federal mineral ownership to start 30 days after a state permit is filed, categorically excluded from further National Environmental Policy Act analysis and without Endangered Species Act or historic preservation consultation.

Includes transparency measures: monthly publication of pending and approved drilling permits and lease nominations, a 30-day Interior report on the causes of permitting delays, and annual staffing reports.

analysis.who_pays: The public would bear the environmental and health costs of expanded drilling on federal land and offshore: weaker and faster environmental reviews, wildlife consultations waived for some drilling, and deemed compliance with marine mammal and endangered species law for offshore seismic surveys. Citizens who live near drill sites, pipelines, or LNG rail routes would lose the practical ability to challenge federal permits — lawsuits would be barred unless filed within 150 days by someone who commented during the public comment period. Communities could no longer rely on states' broad Clean Water Act authority to block or condition pipeline projects. Future presidents would lose the power to protect public land from new fossil fuel leasing without a new act of Congress.
analysis.who_pays_short: Communities near drilling, and future reviewers

drawbacks.text: Stripping the President of the power to pause federal oil, gas, and coal leasing without an act of Congress would take land-use decisions away from the executive and public comment processes and lock in leasing regardless of market conditions, climate goals, or local opposition.

The 150-day filing window and requirement that only prior commenters may sue would make it far harder for communities, conservation groups, and tribes to challenge federal energy permits in court, even for large pipeline or offshore projects.

Categorical exclusions from environmental review for drilling on mixed-ownership land, deemed compliance with the Marine Mammal Protection Act and Endangered Species Act for offshore seismic surveys, and one-year review deadlines would shorten or skip analysis of risks to wildlife, water, and nearby residents.

Protecting the transport of liquefied natural gas by rail from federal prohibition raises safety questions, since refrigerated methane is a hazardous cargo and the bill limits the Transportation Secretary's ability to issue long-term restrictions (short-term emergency orders would remain).

The bill narrows the Clean Water Act's section 401 certification so state objections would be limited to water quality standards in effect under section 303, reducing states' power over interstate pipelines.

Even supporters of faster permitting would acknowledge that requiring all pending drilling permits to be issued within 30 days and processing them despite pending litigation could force decisions before reviews or court questions are resolved.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The streamlining provisions have some genuine merit — hard deadlines, publication of permitting data, and categorical exclusions for routine transmission maintenance would help renewable and grid projects as well as fossil projects, and the transparency reports would show the public where delays come from. But the core of the bill is a large transfer of public land and offshore resources to oil, gas, and coal companies through mandatory lease sales, mandatory permit issuance, and a near-shutdown of citizen lawsuits, paid for with thinner environmental review and less local and state control. On balance the costs to communities, wildlife, and future land-use flexibility outweigh the efficiency gains.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the last months of the session, sent to five committees that never held a hearing or markup, and expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Bruce Westerman introduced the TAP American Energy Act on September 29, 2022, with four Republican cosponsors, including Representative Graves of Missouri.

The bill was referred to five committees — Natural Resources, Agriculture, Transportation and Infrastructure, Energy and Commerce, and Armed Services — with provisions parceled out to subcommittees on Railroads, Pipelines and Hazardous Materials, Energy, and Conservation and Forestry in the following days.
No committee reported the bill, no hearings or markups appear in the record, and the bill never reached the House floor before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal agencies and the communities and conservation interests that rely on environmental review came out ahead, since the mandatory leasing, weakened permitting, and lawsuit limits never took effect. Oil, gas, and pipeline companies gained nothing from the bill itself.

sides.party_line_note: All five sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans, and no vote was ever taken, so there is no roll-call record — but the sponsorship was entirely one party.

industries.note: The bill guarantees frequent onshore and offshore lease sales, forces issuance of all pending drilling permits within 30 days, and lets drilling continue through litigation — the industry's gain in public-land access comes with thinner environmental review for the people living near it.

One-stop federal pipeline reviews, narrowed state Clean Water Act vetoes, protection for LNG-by-rail transport, and a 150-day lawsuit window would all speed projects that communities along the routes would have less power to challenge.
The bill bars any presidential moratorium on new federal coal leases or land withdrawals without an act of Congress, insulating the industry from executive-branch policy changes.

industries.industry: Renewable energy, geothermal, and transmission developers
industries.note: The same streamlining applies to renewables: categorical exclusions for transmission maintenance and storage additions, 50-year right-of-way terms, annual geothermal lease sales, and deadlines for environmental reviews would help build wind, solar, and grid projects faster. This part of the bill's interest runs alongside the public's interest in a working grid.

industries.industry: Federal land conservation and outdoor recreation interests
industries.note: Mandatory leasing across all eligible parcels and the ban on presidential land withdrawals would shrink the ability to keep federal land unleased, and the 150-day, commenter-only lawsuit rule would leave fewer tools to contest sales.
